Q11.answer: The final rule does not state the Form I-539 filing fee or a USCIS processing time. It says the EOS request must include 'the appropriate fee' (8 CFR 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A)) and that the I-539 fee is intended to cover processing (91 FR 45015, lines 5257-5260). Figures in the rule: $233 is the DSO cost per EOS request in DHS's regulatory impact analysis (91 FR 45092); that is a school cost, not a student fee. $420 and $555 appear only in commenters' statements (91 FR 45055, 45065). On processing, DHS states it cannot guarantee processing times (91 FR 45025). A commenter reported USCIS California Service Center averages of 4.5 months for changes of status and 3.5 months for extensions (91 FR 45083), and another reported 6.5 months to adjudicate 80 percent of EOS requests (91 FR 45063); these are commenters' statements, not DHS findings. Draft handout sentence: 'Extension-of-stay applications are filed on Form I-539 with a USCIS filing fee set by the current fee schedule and form instructions; the rule itself does not set the amount. USCIS does not guarantee processing times, and recent commenter-reported processing for extensions has ranged from about three to six months, so file well before your authorized stay ends and keep your receipt notice.'
Q11.basis: 91 FR 44976; 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A) (91 FR 45126); preamble at 91 FR 45015 (fee purpose), 45025 (processing not guaranteed), 45055, 45063, 45065, 45083, 45092.
Q11.uncertainty: The current I-539 fee is set in USCIS fee rules and form instructions, which are outside this record. The commenter figures are not verified by DHS. The 240-day employment window is a separate matter.

Q12.answer: (a) Probably yes. Under 214.1(m)(1), Priya is authorized to remain until the program end date plus 60 days, which is July 14, 2027. An I-539 received on or before July 14, 2027 is timely under 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) read with (m)(1). Filing in days 31-60 is therefore timely on the text. But (f)(7)(iii)(B) and (f)(5)(v) refer to the 30-day period, so the 60-day reading is an inference from (m)(1). (b) No, in practice. Automatic extension under 214.2(f)(5)(viii) covers only on-campus, CPT, and severe economic hardship employment that is otherwise authorized, and it does not apply to filings made during the 30-day period in (f)(5)(v). Her on-campus or CPT employment ends with her program on May 15, 2027 (m)(1), so there is nothing to extend after that date. Recommendation: file the I-539 before May 15, 2027 if she needs continued on-campus or CPT work, which avoids the 30-day window; file no later than July 14, 2027 if she needs status only; do not rely on the 60-day period for timeliness; keep the receipt notice and an endorsed I-20.
Q12.uncertainty: The text does not expressly say that an EOS filed in days 31-60 is timely, or whether the (f)(5)(viii) employment extension applies to a filing in those days. The rule's own language on the 60-day departure period is in (m)(1) only.

Q13.answer: (a) Authorized stay after return: under 214.1(m)(1) (transition), Sofia may remain until the program end date (May 14, 2027) + 60 days = July 13, 2027 (May 14 to May 31 is 17 days; June is 30 days, reaching 47; July 13 is day 60). But because she departed before filing the I-765 and is admitted with a fixed period, 214.1(m)(1)(ii) requires her to file both the I-765 and the I-539. The fixed I-94 date CBP writes on re-entry is not stated in the rule; under 214.2(f)(5)(v) and 214.1(a)(4)(i) it would likely be program end + 30 days = June 13, 2027 (May 14 + 30; May 14 to May 31 is 17 days; June 13 is day 30). Without any filing she is authorized to stay only to the date on the I-94 (June 13 or July 13, 2027, depending on the reading). (b) Yes, under 214.1(m)(1)(ii), because she departed before filing and was admitted with a fixed period, she must file both the I-765 and the I-539 (by cross-reference to 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) or (C)). The safe filing date is on or before June 13, 2027 (the I-94 date; 214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B) applies the 'on or before expiration' rule). (c) If all is approved as requested: the EAD runs June 10, 2027 to June 9, 2028; under 214.1(m)(1)(i), the authorized stay is EAD expiry + 60 days = June 9, 2028 + 60 = August 8, 2028 (June 9 to June 30 is 21 days; July is 31 days, reaching 52; August 8 is day 60). If the I-539 route instead applies the 30-day period of 214.2(f)(5)(v), the date would be July 9, 2028; the rule text is inconsistent here. (d) No I-539 needed. She did not depart before filing, so 214.1(m)(1)(i) exempts the I-539 because the I-765 was filed on or before March 18, 2027. Re-entry: 214.1(m)(1)(ii), last sentence, says a student who departs while an I-765 is pending is admitted under 214.1(a). Under 214.1(a)(4)(iii), a student admitted to pursue OPT while the I-765 is pending may be admitted until the DSO's recommended employment end date on the I-20 plus 30 days: June 9, 2028 + 30 = July 9, 2028 (June 9 to June 30 is 21 days; July 9 is day 30). She should carry the I-797C receipt for the I-765 and the I-20 showing the recommended employment end date (214.1(c)(8)(iii)).
Q13.uncertainty: The text conflicts on whether a student who departed before filing must file an I-539 when she has a timely I-765 (the (m)(1)(i) exemption versus the (m)(1)(ii) requirement); I follow the specific (m)(1)(ii) sentence. The I-94 date on re-entry (30 days versus the 60-day transition period) is not stated. The text for 214.2(f)(11)(i)(B)(2) was not read in full.

Q14.answer: (a) Document: proposed rule 'Optional Practical Training Fees', 2026-20660, 91 FR 64566, published October 8, 2026, type NPRM, agency DHS (ICE), docket ICEB-2026-0100, RIN 1653-AB01. Status: proposed, not final. Deadlines: comments due on or before November 9, 2026 (passed as of today). The proposed rule would take effect 60 days after final publication (91 FR 64577). (b) Probably $70,000, not $30,000, on the text as proposed. The $30,000 subsequent fee applies to a student who previously participated in OPT and for whom the $70,000 initial fee has been paid (proposed 8 CFR 214.13(i)(2)). Daniel's post-completion OPT was approved before the effective date, so the grandfather clause means no fee for that EAD, but a later request on or after the effective date is subject to the fee provisions (91 FR 64578-64579). The proposal does not say how a pre-rule OPT affects the amount, and Daniel did not pay the $70,000 fee, so the $30,000 trigger is not met on the text. The default reading is therefore $70,000; the text is not explicit. (c) The SEVP-certified school pays the fee before the DSO enters the OPT recommendation in SEVIS (proposed 8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)-(ii), 214.13(i)). A DSO may not enter the recommendation without the school's payment, and USCIS will not grant employment authorization before payment (proposed 214.2(f)(11)(iii)). The fee is refundable only in limited cases: the school may request a refund if the student has not received an EAD for which payment was made; once an EAD is received, the initial fee is not refundable. SEVP decides refund requests case by case and its decision is final and not appealable (proposed 214.13(i)(1)-(2); 91 FR 64577). (d) The fee applies to DSO recommendations for OPT dated on or after the effective date (proposed 214.13(i)(3); 91 FR 64577). A recommendation dated before the effective date is outside the fee (91 FR 64578-64579). If Daniel's April 2027 recommendation is dated after the effective date, the fee applies; he would be outside it only if the recommendation were dated before the effective date. (e) Under current rules: Daniel must file Form I-765 for the STEM OPT extension. Because April 12, 2027 is after March 18, 2027, the I-539 exemption in 214.1(m)(1)(i) does not apply, so he should expect to file Form I-539 as well (91 FR 45024: the student may file both concurrently). While the I-765 is pending, a timely and properly filed I-765 automatically extends his EAD until USCIS adjudicates it or 180 days after the prior EAD expires, whichever is earlier (8 CFR 214.2(f)(11)(i)(C), as described in 91 FR 64570 n.51; 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv), not changed by the final rule). Prior EAD expires June 30, 2027; June 30, 2027 + 180 days = December 27, 2027 (July 31 days, Aug 31 days, Sept 30 days, Oct 31 days, Nov 30 days, reaching 153; December 27 is day 180). Stay: if the STEM extension is approved (24 months from July 1, 2027), the stay runs to the EAD end (June 30, 2029) plus 60 days = August 29, 2029 under 214.1(m)(1)(i), or July 30, 2029 under 214.2(f)(5)(v) if the 30-day period applies. The text is not explicit for a late-filed I-765.
Q14.basis: NPRM 2026-20660 (91 FR 64566): DATES and SUMMARY (lines 76-80), discussion of fee amounts and timing (91 FR 64577-64579), footnote 51 on 214.2(f)(11)(i)(C) (91 FR 64570), discussion of 24-month STEM OPT (91 FR 64568). Final rule 2026-14439: 214.1(m)(1)(i) (91 FR 45123); 214.2(f)(5)(viii) (91 FR 45125-45126); preamble on EOS with OPT (91 FR 45024). CFR: 8 CFR 274a.12(b)(6)(iv) (not amended).
Q14.uncertainty: The amount for a student who previously had OPT under the pre-rule regime is not resolved by the proposal. The end date of the stay if approved depends on how the STEM extension is measured and which provision (m)(1)(i) or 214.2(f)(5)(v) governs a late-filed I-765. The proposal could change before finalization.

Q15.answer: 1. Incorrect. The timely-filing rule is that USCIS must receive the EOS on or before the expiration of the authorized period of stay, including the 30-day departure period. The I-20 program end date is not the deadline. Reword: 'USCIS must receive the extension application on or before the expiration of the student's authorized period of stay, which includes the 30-day period after the program end date.' 2. Incorrect. The four-year maximum is counted from the program start date, not the date of entry; the period before the program start date (up to 30 days) and the 30-day departure period do not count. Reword: 'The four-year maximum is counted from the program start date on the I-20.' 3. Partly correct. After 240 days from the I-94 end date, the automatic extension of employment ends, and the student must stop on-campus, CPT and severe-hardship employment. But the stay continues while the timely application is pending and no 240-day limit applies to the stay. Reword: 'If USCIS has not decided a timely filed extension application within 240 days after the I-94 end date, the student may keep studying and remaining in status while the application is pending but must stop authorized employment.' 4. Incorrect as stated. 214.2(f)(5)(i)(A) restricts English language training programs to a maximum admission period of 24 months, with no medical exception in the text. A medical-reason extension ground exists in 214.2(f)(7)(i)(C)(2)(ii), but the text does not say it overrides the 24-month cap, and DHS describes the cap as designed to prevent abuse. Reword: 'English language training students are limited to 24 months; the rule does not provide a medical exception to that cap.' 5. Incorrect. The rule's four-year limit is a screening period, not a completion deadline; the text does not require shortening the program or issuing two I-20s. A student may travel and re-enter with a period of admission to finish, or apply for an extension (91 FR 45001-45002). Reword: 'A program longer than four years is not shortened by the rule; students who need more time apply for an extension or travel and re-enter with a new admission period.' 6. Mostly correct. A student readmitted on a later-dated I-20 after travel can receive a new admission period from CBP and generally does not need an extension for that period, as the preamble notes that travel and re-entry is an alternative to an EOS. Caveats: this assumes no EOS is pending (if one is pending and the student departs and is admitted on a new I-20 with a later end date, the application may be deemed abandoned under 214.1(c)(8)(ii)), and the admission period is limited to the four-year and program-length limits. Reword to include these caveats. 7. Incorrect. The regulation (214.1(m)(1)(i)) sets March 18, 2027 as the last filing date for the Form I-765 exemption from I-539. Six months after September 15, 2026 is March 15, 2027, but the regulatory text controls; the preamble's 'within six months' wording (91 FR 45033) is approximate. The exemption also covers only OPT and STEM OPT applications, not all I-765s. Reword: 'F-1 students who timely file a Form I-765 for post-completion OPT or STEM OPT on or before March 18, 2027 do not need Form I-539 for the requested period.'
Q15.uncertainty: Where the preamble and text differ (item 7: six months versus March 18, 2027), the regulatory text controls. Item 4 is unresolved by the text because the medical ground and the 24-month cap are not reconciled. Item 6 depends on whether the admission period, an EOS, or abandonment is in play.

Q16.answer: (a) Admit-until date: September 22, 2031. The four-year maximum runs from the program start date, not the entry date (91 FR 45016). Program start August 23, 2027 + 4 years = August 23, 2031; + 30 days departure = September 22, 2031 (August 23 to August 31 is 8 days; September 22 is 30 days). The 30 days before program start (she enters August 2, 2027) do not count. (b) She must file an extension of stay (Form I-539) with USCIS, with the DSO-endorsed updated I-20 showing the new program end date, evidence of funds, biometrics, and the fee (214.2(f)(7)(iii)(A)). Grounds: she must have continuously maintained status, be pursuing a full course of study, and have a current I-20 showing additional time or a qualifying reason such as a compelling academic reason (214.2(f)(7)(i)). She may file early: the rule imposes no bar on early filing (91 FR 45027). The application must be received on or before September 22, 2031 (214.2(f)(7)(iii)(B)). If granted in full, the stay runs to the program end date plus 30 days: May 14, 2033 + 30 = June 13, 2033 (May 14 to May 31 is 17 days; June 13 is day 30). The extension cannot exceed 4 years (214.2(f)(7)(vi)); the 4-year cap is the stated limit, and the program end date controls here. (c) The master's degree in 2029 does not by itself bar finishing the PhD in F-1 status. The rule bars same or lower level programs after completing a program after September 15, 2026 (214.2(f)(5)(ii)(C)); a PhD is a higher level, and 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(B) allows progression to a higher level. But the change of educational objective must be handled: 214.2(f)(5)(ii)(A) bars a graduate student from changing educational objectives at any point during the program, subject to SEVP exceptions, and (D) requires an EOS on the USCIS form when such a change is sought. The rule does not say whether the master's conferral within the PhD program is such a change. (d) She may be admitted for a period up to her unexpired I-94 (September 22, 2031) and in any event not beyond the 4-year-from-program-start limit plus 30 days, which is September 22, 2031. Her 2030 readmission does not remove the need to file under (b) before September 22, 2031 if she wants to remain past that date. The certainty of the admission period is limited: the rule does not expressly address re-entry with an unexpired I-94 and no pending EOS. (e) Her husband's authorized stay may not exceed Lin's authorized period (214.2(f)(5)(i)(E); 91 FR 45016-45017), so his stay ends at Lin's I-94 date, September 22, 2031, even if his own I-94 shows a later date. When Lin applies under (b), he must be included in her EOS or file his own, and it must be received on or before the expiration of his previously authorized period, which is capped at Lin's date (214.2(f)(7)(iv)). The Form I-539 allows dependents to be included for one fee (91 FR 45013-45014 preamble). The rule does not set the fee amount.
Q16.uncertainty: The text does not say whether an extension can exceed the 4-year cap measured from program start; I read the cap as applying to the total stay and the program end date as controlling. The rule does not say how a master's conferral within a PhD affects the EOS. The fee for the I-539 and any dependent fee is not in the rule. Re-entry with an unexpired I-94 and no pending EOS is not expressly addressed.
